title: Newar Buddhism
hook: in Nepal's Kathmandu Valley, a Sanskrit Buddhism with householder priests

segments.voice: Yesterday, many Nichiren communities, and a rule for hearing them. Your line was each speaks for itself. Whose own words did you go and find? Day one thousand three hundred forty-five.

A narrow doorway off a busy street, and suddenly a courtyard. Pigeons on old paving stones. Laundry on a balcony. Children cutting across on their way to school. At the far end, a shrine, and in front of it a man in ordinary clothes, a husband and a father, ringing a small bell and reciting in Sanskrit. He is a priest. His family says his father was one too, and his father's father. The courtyard around him is still called a monastery, though families live along its edges. This is the Kathmandu Valley in Nepal. Today: Newar Buddhism.
screen: `A DOORWAY, THEN A COURTYARD.` → `A FATHER RINGING A BELL.` → `STILL CALLED A MONASTERY.`

segments.voice: First, who. The Newars are the people of the Kathmandu Valley, with their own language, their own cities, and their own old crafts of metal, wood and painting. Some Newars are Buddhist, some Hindu, and in the valley the two share streets, festivals and sometimes the same holy places. Second, the language. Newar Buddhism is a Mahayana and Vajrayana tradition whose sacred texts and rituals are in Sanskrit. The valley's monasteries copied and recited Sanskrit Buddhist texts, and those texts are still read and honored in its temples today. Third, the priests. Elsewhere on this path, the central figures were often monks who left home. Here, the ritual heart of the tradition belongs to householders. The Vajracharyas, whose name means vajra masters, are married priests who perform rites for families, and the Shakyas, whose name, tradition says, is the name of the Buddha's own clan, keep the shrines with them. A boy from these families goes through a monastic ordination rite, wears the robes for a short time, and then returns to household life, carrying the monastery with him. Fourth, the courtyard and the festival. A baha or bahi is a courtyard monastery, built around a shrine, with families living along its sides. And at festival time, in the city of Patan, a towering chariot carrying Karunamaya, the compassionate one, is pulled through the streets by crowds, Buddhist and Hindu together. Put it all together and you get a religion that lives in a neighborhood, handed down at the dinner table as much as in the temple: the valley's way.
screen: `THE PEOPLE OF THE VALLEY.` · `SANSKRIT TEXTS AND RITES.` · `HOUSEHOLDER PRIESTS.` · `THE COURTYARD AND THE CHARIOT.` · then, large: `THE VALLEY'S WAY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing your family has done for longer than you have been alive. A recipe. A song. A way of setting the table, lighting a lamp, or naming a child. If an object tied to it is nearby, hold it in your hands. Picture the hands that did this before yours, one pair behind another, as far back as you can see. You don't have to keep the tradition to honor it. Just let the line of hands be there with you, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Newar Buddhism. The Buddhism of the Newar people of Nepal's Kathmandu Valley: Sanskrit texts, courtyard monasteries, and married householder priests. Today's word.
Your line: the valley's way. Today, ask one older relative or friend how something was done when they were young, and listen to the whole answer. Day one thousand three hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Newar Buddhists in Nepal's Kathmandu Valley worship at courtyard monasteries (bahas), with rituals in Sanskrit led by married, hereditary Vajracharya priests; boys of Vajracharya and Shakya families pass through a brief monastic ordination before returning to household life.
